passage:
Hemant: are you doing the group dance at the function
Omkar: yes!! but my palms are sweaty already 😅
Hemant: you love it though
Omkar: I do. when we all move together I feel like I belong, you know?
Hemant: yeah I get that
Omkar: but Kabir said I should skip it because 'boys don't do that'
Hemant: did that change your mind
Omkar: it made me feel a bit small for a day
Omkar: then I thought no. it's my choice
Hemant: good. I'll stand at the back and clap for you
Omkar: come on the stage
Hemant: ...ok fine, I'll dance badly 🙂

qa.q: Which event is Omkar going to dance at?
qa.a: Omkar is going to dance at the function.

qa.q: What is Omkar feeling about the dance, and what mixed feelings show?
qa.a: Omkar feels joy and belonging when they move together, and some nerves too, since the palms are sweaty. Omkar felt small after Kabir's remark before deciding it was a personal choice.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if someone teases about dancing?
qa.a: Omkar can remember it's a personal choice and lean on friends who back the decision. Omkar can also tell a trusted adult if teasing turns unkind.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel about being asked onto the stage?
qa.a: Hemant seems shy about dancing but agrees to join Omkar. Choice matters for Hemant too.

grounding: A teenager dances in a group to show joy and belonging, and teasing shows why choice matters.

passage: The village wedding baraat came down the lane in a haze of dust and drums. Binita's cousins pulled her into the circle, and she found herself laughing and stepping in time, arms up, feet quick. She felt part of everything. Then Divyansh, watching from a scooter, called out, "Look at her moves, she's a film star!" in a teasing sing-song. Binita's steps faltered. Her face went hot and she slipped to the edge. Divyansh saw it and walked over. "Sorry, I only meant it as a joke. You looked great." After a while she stepped back in, at her own pace.

qa.q: How did the baraat come down the lane?
qa.a: It came down in a haze of dust and drums.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling as she danced, and after Divyansh's remark?
qa.a: She felt joy and belonging while dancing. After the teasing she felt embarrassed, as her steps faltered and her face went hot.

qa.q: What went right when Divyansh walked over?
qa.a: Divyansh apologised and said Binita looked great, which let Binita choose to dance again. Divyansh noticed the effect of the joke.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have seen Divyansh's own comment at first?
qa.a: Divyansh meant it as a friendly joke, and did not expect it to shame her. Seeing her go to the edge changed that.

grounding: A teenager dances at a wedding baraat for joy and belonging, and teasing can turn joy to shame while choice restores it.

passage:
At the school's cultural evening in Lisbon, Kwame took the stage with a dance his grandmother had taught him back in Ghana: quick feet, shoulders rolling, a big grin.
A few boys at the back snickered. "What is that?"
Kwame's smile faltered. He glanced at the teachers.
Then Paulo, his friend from football, stood up and started clapping to the beat. A few others joined. Paulo jumped on stage and tried to copy the steps, badly.
Kwame laughed and slowed down to show him.
By the end, six kids were on stage, all trying the dance. Kwame's grin was back, bigger than ever.
Afterwards, Paulo said, "Teach me properly next week?"
"Only if you want to," Kwame said. "Dancing's better when you choose it."

qa.q: Who taught Kwame the dance?
qa.a: His grandmother, back in Ghana.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling when the boys snickered?
qa.a: Kwame felt embarrassed and unsure, his joy turning into worry about being mocked.

qa.q: What did Paulo do that helped?
qa.a: Paulo clapped along and joined the dance, turning the teasing moment into shared fun and belonging.

qa.q: How might the boys at the back see the dance after others joined in?
qa.a: They might see it as something fun and cool, not strange, once the group showed support.

grounding: At a school event, a teenager's cultural dance shows joy and belonging, teasing threatens it, and a friend's support restores it.

passage:
At the Class 10 annual day rehearsal, the dance teacher, Mrs Rao, pointed at Kashish. "You're in the front row for the group dance."
Kashish's face went pale. "Ma'am, I don't want to dance. Can I do something else?"
"Everyone dances. It's fun!"
Kashish looked at the floor, arms tight at her sides.
Devika, standing nearby, spoke up. "Ma'am, Kashish is great with the lights. Could she do that?"
Mrs Rao paused, then nodded. "Fine. Lights."
On the night, Kashish ran the lights perfectly, grinning each time the stage glowed. In the last song, she even swayed along from the control desk, by her own choice.

qa.q: What job did Kashish do on the night?
qa.a: She ran the lights.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when told to dance in the front row?
qa.a: Kashish felt anxious and pressured, not wanting to dance in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Devika do that helped?
qa.a: Devika suggested another role for Kashish, respecting her choice not to dance.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Kashish's swaying at the end?
qa.a: Mrs Rao might realise that Kashish enjoyed the music in her own way when she wasn't forced.

grounding: At school, a teenager is pressured to dance, a friend supports her choice, and joy returns when she chooses how to join.

passage:
Dear Uma Didi,
Guess what? At Rinku Bhaiya's wedding, I danced in the baraat! You always said I should.
At first, some of the boys teased, "Girls don't dance in front!" I almost stepped back. My face was hot.
But then Nani came out, grabbed my hand, and started dancing with me. Everyone cheered. I danced all the way to the gate. My feet hurt, but I felt so happy, like I really belonged with the family.
Some of the aunties even joined us. It was the best part of the whole wedding.
Next time you have to come and dance too!
Love,
Trisha

qa.q: Who grabbed Trisha's hand and started dancing?
qa.a: Nani.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when the boys teased?
qa.a: Trisha felt embarrassed and hesitant, almost stepping back from dancing.

qa.q: What helped Trisha keep dancing?
qa.a: Nani joining in and the family cheering gave Trisha courage and a sense of belonging.

qa.q: If you were Uma Didi, how might this letter feel?
qa.a: You might feel proud and happy that Trisha danced and felt part of the family.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager describes dancing at a baraat, overcoming teasing about gender norms, and feeling joy and belonging.

passage: Mridul, you keep asking why I didn't dance at the fest when you've seen me dance at my cousin's baraat. Okay, here's Kiran's full explanation, one time only. At the baraat it was dhol, dust, my Tauji's terrible bhangra, and all my cousins pulling me in. Nobody filmed me, nobody cared if I was good. I danced for two hours and felt I belonged to every person on that road. The fest was different. Some seniors said the dance team was "a girls' thing" and started calling the boys who joined silly names. Nobody forced me out, but it didn't feel like choosing either. So I sat out. And I hated sitting out. Next year, if you join with me, I'll do it. Deal? It's my dancing. It's not theirs to decide.

qa.q: How long did Kiran dance at the baraat?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while dancing at the baraat?
qa.a: Kiran felt joyful and part of the whole family, free because nobody was filming or judging.

qa.q: What turned dancing from joy into something Kiran avoided at the fest?
qa.a: The seniors' teasing about gender and the names they called the boys, which made joining feel risky rather than a free choice.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel about Kiran's "Deal?"
qa.a: Mridul may feel trusted and glad to help, since joining together could make dancing feel like Kiran's own choice again.

grounding: It illustrates dance as joy and belonging at a family baraat, and gender-based teasing turning it into something avoided, with choice at the centre.
